title: Control and Coordination
subject: science
syllabus_note: Follows the CBSE 2025-26 syllabus: tropic movements in plants; introduction of plant hormones; control and coordination in animals: nervous system; voluntary, involuntary and reflex action; chemical coordination: animal hormones.

blocks.title: Catch!
blocks.body:
A friend throws a ball to you without warning. In less than a second your eyes see it, your brain works out where it will go, your arm moves, and your fingers close around it.

Many organs worked together, in the right order, very fast. This is **control and coordination**. Animals use the **nervous system** and **hormones**; plants, which have no nerves, use **chemicals** alone. In this chapter you will learn how both work.

blocks.title: He showed that plants respond
blocks.body:
Jagadish Chandra Bose of Bengal was a physicist and a plant scientist. He built the **crescograph**, an instrument that could magnify the tiny growth of a plant thousands of times, and showed that plants respond to touch, light and other stimuli with electrical signals, much as animal tissues do.

He was also a pioneer of radio and microwave research. The Bose Institute in Kolkata, which he founded in 1917, still carries on his work.
blocks.future: The study of nerves, hormones and plant responses leads to careers in medicine, neuroscience, psychology, sports science, agriculture and plant biotechnology.

blocks.question: You touch a very hot plate and pull your hand back before you even feel the pain. Which part decided to move your hand?
options: The muscles of the hand themselves
blocks.explanation: This is a reflex action: the decision is made in the spinal cord, which is quicker than sending the signal up to the brain and waiting for thinking.

blocks.title: Neurons and reflexes
blocks.body:
The nervous system is made of nerve cells, **neurons**. Information from the environment is detected by **receptors**, for example in the inner ear (hearing and balance), nose (smell), tongue (taste) and eyes (sight).

**How a message travels:**
1. Information reaches the tip of a **dendrite** and starts a chemical reaction that creates an **electrical impulse**.
2. The impulse travels from the dendrite to the **cell body**, and then along the **axon** to its end.
3. At the end of the axon, the impulse releases chemicals. These cross the gap between two neurons, the **synapse**, and start a similar impulse in the dendrite of the next neuron.
4. Finally the message reaches a muscle or gland (the **effector**), which acts.

A **reflex action** is a sudden, automatic response to a stimulus, done without thinking, such as pulling back the hand from a flame. Its path is the **reflex arc**: receptor → sensory neuron → relay neuron in the **spinal cord** → motor neuron → effector (muscle). Reflex arcs are formed in the spinal cord, so the response is quick; the information also goes on to the brain.

blocks.question: The gap between two neurons, where chemicals carry the message across, is called the:
blocks.explanation: At the synapse, chemicals released by the axon ending start a new impulse in the next neuron.
option_feedback: The axon carries the impulse away from the cell body.
The cell body has the nucleus.

blocks.title: Three parts of the brain
blocks.body:
The brain and the spinal cord form the **central nervous system**. The nerves from them to all parts of the body form the **peripheral nervous system**.

- **Fore-brain:** the main thinking part. It has areas that receive sensory impulses (hearing, smell, sight), areas that control voluntary muscles, and areas that store information. It also has the centre for **hunger**.
- **Mid-brain** and **hind-brain:** control many **involuntary** actions. The **medulla** in the hind-brain controls blood pressure, salivation and vomiting. The **cerebellum** in the hind-brain controls **posture and balance** and the precision of voluntary actions, such as walking in a straight line, riding a bicycle or picking up a pencil.

**Protection:** the brain sits inside a bony box, the **skull**, cushioned by a fluid-filled balloon that absorbs shocks. The spinal cord is protected by the **vertebral column** (backbone).

**Movement:** when a nerve impulse reaches a muscle, special proteins in the muscle cells change their shape and arrangement, and the muscle fibre becomes shorter.

blocks.question: Which part of the brain maintains posture and balance of the body?
blocks.explanation: The cerebellum, in the hind-brain, controls posture, balance and the precision of voluntary actions.
option_feedback: The medulla controls blood pressure, salivation and vomiting.
The pons is part of the hind-brain but does not control balance.

blocks.title: Movements without nerves
blocks.body:
Plants have neither a nervous system nor muscles. They respond to stimuli in two ways:

**1. Immediate movement, not due to growth.** The leaves of the **sensitive plant** (touch-me-not, Mimosa) fold up when touched. Plant cells pass the information from cell to cell electrically and chemically; the cells then change shape by changing the amount of water in them, so they swell or shrink.

**2. Slow movement due to growth (tropisms):** the direction of growth depends on the stimulus.
- **Phototropism** (light): shoots bend towards light; roots grow away from it.
- **Geotropism** (gravity): roots grow downwards; shoots grow upwards.
- **Hydrotropism** (water): roots grow towards water.
- **Chemotropism** (chemicals): pollen tubes grow towards the ovules.

**How a shoot bends towards light:** the hormone **auxin** is made at the shoot tip. When light comes from one side, auxin diffuses to the shady side. There it makes the cells grow longer, so the shoot bends towards the light. In the same way, a **tendril** coils around a support: the part away from the support grows faster than the part touching it.

blocks.title: Plant hormones
blocks.body:
| Hormone | Main effect |
|---|---|
| Auxin | made at the shoot tip; makes cells grow longer (bending towards light, tendrils coiling) |
| Gibberellins | help in the growth of the stem |
| Cytokinins | promote cell division; present in fruits and seeds |
| Abscisic acid | inhibits growth; causes wilting of leaves |

blocks.question: A plant hormone that inhibits growth and causes wilting of leaves is:
blocks.explanation: Abscisic acid inhibits growth; the other three promote growth or cell division.

blocks.title: Chemical messengers
blocks.body:
**Hormones** are chemicals made by **endocrine glands** and released directly into the **blood**, which carries them to all parts of the body. They act only on cells that have the right receptors.

**Adrenaline** from the adrenal glands prepares the body for an emergency (fight or flight): the heart beats faster to supply more oxygen to the muscles, blood to the digestive system and skin is reduced, blood is diverted to the skeletal muscles, and breathing becomes faster because the diaphragm and rib muscles contract more.

**Iodised salt** is advised because iodine is needed to make **thyroxin**. Without enough iodine, a person may suffer from **goitre**, a swollen neck.

**Insulin** from the pancreas lowers the blood sugar level. If it is not secreted in proper amounts, sugar in the blood rises (**diabetes**); such patients are given injections of insulin.

blocks.title: Endocrine glands and their hormones
blocks.body:
| Gland | Hormone | Function |
|---|---|---|
| Hypothalamus | releasing hormones | control the release of hormones from the pituitary |
| Pituitary | growth hormone | growth and development (too little: dwarfism; too much: gigantism) |
| Thyroid | thyroxin (needs iodine) | metabolism of carbohydrates, proteins and fats (lack of iodine: goitre) |
| Pancreas | insulin | lowers the blood sugar level (too little: diabetes) |
| Adrenal | adrenaline | prepares the body for emergencies |
| Testes | testosterone | changes at puberty in boys |
| Ovaries | oestrogen | changes at puberty in girls |

blocks.question: Which hormone needs iodine for its synthesis?
blocks.explanation: The thyroid gland needs iodine to make thyroxin; lack of iodine can cause goitre.
option_feedback: Growth hormone does not need iodine.
Insulin is made by the pancreas without iodine.

blocks.title: Feedback and comparison
blocks.body:
**Feedback mechanism:** the timing and amount of a hormone are regulated by feedback. For example, when the sugar level in the blood rises, cells of the pancreas detect it and secrete more insulin; as the sugar level falls, insulin secretion is reduced.

| Nervous control | Hormonal control |
|---|---|
| electrical impulses along nerves | chemicals carried in the blood |
| very fast | slower |
| reaches only cells connected by nerves | reaches all cells of the body |
| short-lived; a cell needs time to reset | steady and long-lasting |

blocks.question: Which of these is true of hormonal control compared with nervous control?
options: It reaches all cells of the body through the blood
It reaches only cells connected by nerves
blocks.explanation: Hormones travel in the blood and reach every cell; nerve impulses are faster but reach only the cells they are connected to.
option_feedback: Nerves use electrical impulses; hormones are chemicals.

blocks.title: Remember the path and the parts
blocks.body:
- **Reflex arc:** **R**eceptor → **S**ensory → **R**elay (spinal cord) → **M**otor → **E**ffector: "**R**ats **S**ometimes **R**un **M**any **E**rrands".
- **Hind-brain:** **C**erebellum = **C**ontrol of balance; **M**edulla = **M**achine jobs (blood pressure, salivation, vomiting).
- **Plant hormones:** **A**uxin = **A**rches towards light; **G**ibberellin = **G**rows stem; **C**ytokinin = **C**ell division; **A**bscisic acid = **A**rrests growth.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.body:
- Writing that reflex actions are controlled by the brain: the reflex arc is in the spinal cord.
- Saying that Mimosa leaves fold because of growth: they fold because cells lose water and change shape.
- Writing that insulin is made by the pituitary: it is made by the pancreas.
- Mixing up dendrite and axon: the impulse goes dendrite → cell body → axon.
- Writing that the cerebrum controls balance: the cerebellum does.

blocks.title: Try it in class
blocks.body: Do the ruler-drop test: one student holds a ruler, another catches it when it falls; the distance shows reaction time. Tap below the knee to show the knee-jerk reflex. Grow a seedling in a box with a hole on one side to show phototropism over a week, and bring a touch-me-not plant to class.

blocks.title: Explain it in your own words
blocks.body: Explain to a friend how your body reacts when a dog suddenly barks at you: which actions are reflexes, which are controlled by the brain, and what adrenaline does.

blocks.title: Where this leads
blocks.body:
- **Chapter 5:** adrenaline changes breathing and heartbeat; insulin controls the use of glucose.
- **Chapter 7, How do Organisms Reproduce?:** testosterone and oestrogen bring changes at puberty.
- **Class 11 and 12 Biology:** neural control, chemical coordination and plant growth regulators in detail.

blocks.title: Mastery challenge
blocks.body:
A potted plant is kept near a window. After a week its shoot has bent towards the window. The pot is then turned around by 180°.

(a) What will happen to the shoot over the next few days? (b) Which hormone is responsible, and where is it made? (c) Will the roots respond in the same way?

**Answer:** (a) The shoot will bend back towards the window, because the light now comes from the other side. (b) Auxin, made at the shoot tip; it moves to the shady side and makes those cells grow longer. (c) No: roots are negatively phototropic and grow away from light, mainly responding to gravity and water.

blocks.title: Chapter summary
blocks.body:
- Control and coordination are done by the nervous system and hormones in animals, and by chemicals in plants.
- A message travels as an electrical impulse from dendrite to cell body to axon, and crosses the synapse as chemicals.
- Reflex actions are fast, automatic and controlled by the spinal cord through the reflex arc.
- The fore-brain is for thinking; the medulla controls involuntary actions; the cerebellum controls posture and balance.
- Plants respond by quick movements (Mimosa) or by growth (tropisms), using hormones such as auxin, gibberellins, cytokinins and abscisic acid.
- Endocrine glands release hormones into the blood; their amount is regulated by feedback.

blocks.title: Board exam tips
blocks.body:
- Practise labelled diagrams of a neuron, the reflex arc and the human brain.
- Learn the endocrine glands table: gland, hormone, function, and the disorder when it goes wrong.
- In tropism answers, name the stimulus, the direction of growth, and the hormone.
- Use a table for differences: nervous vs hormonal control, Mimosa movement vs growth movement.
